newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer-3.0 discussion clouds German EMU debate.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer-3.0 discussion clouds German EMU debate.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer on Wednesday said debate in Germany over the introduction of the euro was being obscured by a dispute over precise adherence to the Maastricht deficit criterion.

Adressing Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber during a Bundesbank reception, Tietmeyer said both houses of parliament had insisted as early as December 1992 that sustainable adherence to the entry criteria was crucial to the project.

Departing from the text of his speech, Tietmeyer said Stoiber was right to insist that the preconditions for the transitions to the single currency had to be right, but added: "I have the impression that the zero discussion has completely obscured the substance of the issue."

Tietmeyer was referring to the debate about whether the Maastricht requirement that government deficits be limited to three percent of gross domestic product should be interpreted as 3.0 precisely, as demanded by Stoiber.
Stoiber has led a campaign for strict adherence to the Maastricht convergence criteria and wants the euro delayed if the deficit goal is not met exactly.
Pressure from Stoiber forced Chancellor Helmut Kohl last week to say three meant 3.0, making it more difficult for Germany to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Tietmeyer read out sentences from a text agreed by both houses of the German federal parliament in 1992 which stressed that the choice of EMU members had to be based on proven stability, convergence on economic fundamentals and sustainable budgetary and fiscal solidity.

"This is not a decision of the Bundesbank nor a decision of the Bavarian state government. This is a decision of both houses of the federal parliament. It is an important orientation for the future for us all," he said.
